title: Ulnar nerve examination: elbow versus wrist lesion

guidelineVersions: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition (2023)

related.why: Applied anatomy of the hand: median and ulnar nerves and the carpal tunnel
Hand examination for Dupuytren's disease or the rheumatoid hand, another focused hand examination

brief.scenario: Mr Daniel Prentiss, 45, has numbness in the little and ring fingers and weakness of grip.
brief.task: Examine the ulnar nerve and try to localise a lesion to the elbow or the wrist.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Look for wasting and clawing, then work through sensation, motor testing and Froment sign before localising with elbow and wrist provocation tests.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Froment sign tests the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve, and a normal dorsal ulnar sensation doesn't tell you much about a wrist-level lesion.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Could you hold both hands out for me, palms down?"

grid.label: Preparation and inspection
grid.fail: Starts testing power without first inspecting both hands and forearms.
grid.pass: Introduces self, gains consent, exposes both hands and forearms, and inspects for hypothenar and first dorsal interosseous wasting.
grid.high: Also looks specifically for clawing of the ring and little fingers before touching the hand.

grid.label: Sensory testing
grid.fail: Tests sensation only on the palmar little finger, or skips sensory testing entirely.
grid.pass: Tests sensation in the ulnar distribution on both the palmar and dorsal aspects of the hand.
grid.high: Explicitly compares dorsal ulnar sensation with palmar ulnar sensation as part of localising the lesion.

grid.label: Motor testing and Froment sign
grid.fail: Tests sensation only, or calls Froment sign a test of the median nerve.
grid.pass: Tests finger abduction and adduction against resistance and performs Froment sign correctly.
grid.high: Explains Froment sign is positive because weak adductor pollicis causes compensatory thumb flexion through flexor pollicis longus.

grid.label: Localising to elbow or wrist
grid.fail: Assumes every ulnar neuropathy is at the elbow without examining for a wrist-level lesion.
grid.pass: Assesses the elbow for tenderness or a Tinel sign over the cubital tunnel and symptoms with elbow flexion, and examines the wrist and ulnar canal.
grid.high: States a lesion at the elbow can affect the dorsal ulnar hand, while a wrist-level lesion may spare dorsal sensation depending on which branch is involved.

grid.label: Deep motor branch at the wrist
grid.fail: States a wrist-level lesion always causes the same pattern as an elbow lesion.
grid.pass: Recognises that the deep motor branch can be affected at the wrist and cause weakness without sensory loss.
grid.high: Explains localisation depends on the specific combination of motor and sensory findings, not any single test.

grid.label: Excluding a more proximal lesion
grid.fail: Doesn't examine the median or radial nerves, or the cervical spine.
grid.pass: Assesses median and radial nerve function and examines the cervical spine to consider a more proximal lesion.
grid.high: Asks specifically about previous trauma, fracture, a ganglion or repetitive pressure at the elbow or wrist as contributing causes.

grid.label: Presentation and localisation
grid.fail: Presents findings without committing to a likely level of the lesion.
grid.pass: Presents key findings and states whether the pattern fits an elbow or wrist lesion, based on the combination of signs.
grid.high: Explains the reasoning behind the localisation explicitly, referencing the specific sensory and motor findings that support it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Goes straight to testing grip strength without inspecting.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Tests only palmar sensation of the little finger.]

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Could this be at the wrist?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, ulnar neuropathy is always at the elbow.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What if there's weakness but no numbness?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That wouldn't happen with an ulnar nerve problem.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, the ulnar nerve tells me everything.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Ulnar nerve problem. Not sure where.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello Mr Prentiss, I'm Dr Patel. Could you hold both hands out, palms down, so I can look at them? [Inspects for hypothenar and first dorsal interosseous wasting.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Tests light touch on both the palmar and dorsal aspects of the ulnar one and a half fingers.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Please spread your fingers and stop me pushing them together. [Tests abduction and adduction.] Now hold this paper between your thumb and finger while I pull it. [Froment sign.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's an ulnar nerve test, not median; a positive sign means weak thumb adduction.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Checks for tenderness and Tinel sign over the cubital tunnel and symptoms on elbow flexion, then examines the wrist and Guyon's canal.]

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if there were weakness but sensation was normal?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That could mean the deep motor branch is affected at the wrist, sparing sensation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Checks median and radial nerve function, and screens the cervical spine.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Reduced sensation in the ulnar one and a half fingers on both palmar and dorsal surfaces, weak finger abduction and a positive Froment sign, with tenderness and a positive Tinel sign at the elbow. This fits an ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello Mr Prentiss, I'm Dr Patel. Could you hold both hands out, palms down? [Inspects for hypothenar and first dorsal interosseous wasting, and specifically looks for clawing of the ring and little fingers.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Tests palmar and dorsal ulnar sensation and compares the two sides directly.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Please spread your fingers against my hand. [Tests abduction/adduction.] Hold this paper. [Froment sign positive.] This happens because weak adductor pollicis makes you compensate by flexing the thumb with flexor pollicis longus.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Assesses the cubital tunnel for tenderness, Tinel sign and symptoms with elbow flexion, and the wrist for a mass or tenderness over Guyon's canal.] Dorsal sensory loss would point to a lesion at or above the wrist, since the dorsal branch leaves before Guyon's canal; a purely wrist-level lesion can spare it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What if there's weakness but sensation is normal?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The deep motor branch can be affected in isolation at the wrist, giving weakness without sensory loss; localisation depends on the whole pattern, not one test.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Checks median and radial nerve function and the cervical spine.] I'd also ask about previous trauma, a fracture, a ganglion, or repetitive pressure at the elbow or wrist.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Reduced sensation on both palmar and dorsal ulnar aspects, weak intrinsic hand muscles, a positive Froment sign, and elbow tenderness with a positive Tinel sign. Since the dorsal branch is affected too, this localises to the elbow rather than the wrist, where dorsal sensation would usually be spared.

failures.move: Calling Froment sign a test of the median nerve.
failures.consequence: Misattributes a positive finding and can misdirect the localisation.

failures.move: Assuming every ulnar neuropathy is at the elbow without examining the wrist.
failures.consequence: A wrist-level or Guyon's canal lesion, such as a ganglion, is missed.

failures.move: Not looking for wasting or clawing before testing power.
failures.consequence: Chronic denervation signs are missed, understating the severity or chronicity of the lesion.

failures.move: Not examining the cervical spine or other nerves.
failures.consequence: A more proximal lesion, such as a cervical radiculopathy, is missed.

recovery.line: I should also test sensation on the dorsal aspect of the hand, since that helps localise the lesion.

recovery.when: Asked why you tested the median nerve too
recovery.line: To exclude a more proximal or combined lesion, since ulnar findings alone don't rule that out.

knowledge.fact: Ulnar neuropathy: inspect for hypothenar and first dorsal interosseous wasting and clawing of the ring and little fingers; test sensation in the ulnar distribution, finger abduction/adduction, and Froment sign.
Froment sign is positive when weak adductor pollicis is compensated by thumb flexion through flexor pollicis longus.

The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises proximal to the wrist; sparing of dorsal sensation with a wrist-level lesion, and its involvement with a more proximal lesion, helps localisation.
The deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve can be affected in isolation at the wrist, causing weakness without sensory loss.

recall.think: Is this ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, at the wrist, or is it more proximal?
recall.say: "Dorsal sensory loss with the motor and elbow findings localises this to the elbow."
do: Sensation both aspects, motor and Froment sign
Elbow and wrist provocation; check median/radial and neck
recall.trap: Froment sign tests the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve.
recall.finish: Localise from the whole pattern; refer for nerve conduction studies and surgical opinion if the level is uncertain or symptoms progress.

partner.opening: Please examine this gentleman's ulnar nerve and try to localise the lesion. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Daniel Prentiss, 45, a delivery driver. Numbness in the little and ring fingers for a few months, worse leaning on your elbow. Weak grip when gripping the steering wheel. No neck pain. No previous fracture or surgery, but you rest your elbow on the car window a lot at work.

reveals.finding: Mild wasting of the hypothenar eminence and first dorsal interosseous on the affected side; slight clawing of the ring and little fingers.
Reduced sensation on both the palmar and dorsal aspects of the little and ring fingers.

reveals.trigger: Tests finger abduction/adduction and Froment sign
reveals.finding: Weak finger abduction and adduction; Froment sign positive.
Tender over the cubital tunnel with a positive Tinel sign; symptoms reproduced on sustained elbow flexion.

reveals.trigger: Examines the wrist and Guyon's canal
reveals.finding: No mass or tenderness at the wrist.

reveals.trigger: Examines median/radial nerves and the neck
reveals.finding: Normal median and radial nerve function; full, pain-free neck movement.

push.question: Why is Froment sign positive?
push.expect: Weak adductor pollicis causes compensatory thumb flexion through flexor pollicis longus.

push.question: What finding suggests a lesion proximal to the wrist rather than at it?
push.expect: Dorsal ulnar sensory loss, since the dorsal branch arises proximal to Guyon's canal.

push.question: How would a deep motor branch lesion at the wrist present differently?
push.expect: Weakness of ulnar-innervated intrinsics without sensory loss, since the deep motor branch can be affected in isolation.

curveballs.prompt: Sensation is normal but there's marked weakness of the intrinsic muscles.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suggests a deep motor branch lesion at the wrist rather than at the elbow.

curveballs.prompt: He mentions a firm lump at the wrist over the ulnar side.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Raises suspicion of a ganglion compressing the nerve in Guyon's canal; examine and consider imaging or surgical referral.

curveballs.prompt: He also has neck pain radiating down the arm.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Raises concern for a more proximal cause such as cervical radiculopathy; examine the neck and consider imaging if findings support it.

curveballs.prompt: The examiner asks whether nerve conduction studies would help.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes, they can help confirm and localise the lesion, especially when clinical findings are equivocal.
